entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Peter Waldo, a prosperous merchant from Lyon, France, in the latter half of the 12th century, initiated a radical religious movement that profoundly challenged the established authority and material wealth of the Roman Catholic Church. Renouncing his considerable fortune around 1173, Waldo embraced a life of apostolic poverty and preaching, advocating for direct access to scripture in vernacular languages and a return to what he perceived as the simplicity of early Christianity. His actions sparked the Waldensian movement, an enduring proto-Protestant tradition that, despite relentless persecution, persisted for centuries across various European regions, making him a pivotal figure in the history of religious dissent and social reform during the High Middle Ages.

Waldo's transformation began with a spiritual crisis, reportedly inspired by the legend of Saint Alexius and a sermon on Matthew 19:21 ('If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor'). After providing for his wife and daughters, he distributed his remaining wealth to the poor and commissioned scholars to translate portions of the Bible, including the Gospels, into the local Franco-Provençal dialect. He and his followers, known initially as the "Poor Men of Lyon," began preaching publicly, emphasizing personal piety, voluntary poverty, and adherence to the Sermon on the Mount. Initially tolerated by the Archbishop of Lyon, their unauthorized preaching led to their condemnation by Pope Alexander III at the Third Lateran Council in 1179 and subsequent excommunication by Pope Lucius III at the Council of Verona in 1184, forcing the movement underground and into widespread evangelism across southern France and Italy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Peter Waldo's movement, Waldensianism, represented one of the earliest and most enduring challenges to the Roman Catholic Church, influencing later reformers and demonstrating the resilience of religious dissent for centuries. His emphasis on vernacular scripture and lay preaching had a lasting impact on European religious thought.
